name: Losing body fat to raise testosterone

lead: Men cut body fat for visible leanness and also because fat tissue converts testosterone to estrogen, so a lower body fat is expected to bring hormones along with the physique.

Fat cells make aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to estradiol, so less fat is proposed to mean less conversion. Wikipedia's testosterone article says weight loss may raise testosterone, and adds that no clear link between body mass index and testosterone has been found.

paras: People pursue it through a calorie deficit, higher protein and resistance training to keep muscle while fat comes off, tracking progress over weeks to months. Some pair it with bloodwork to see whether testosterone shifts.
No specific harms are described in the sources reviewed. The usual considerations of rapid or extreme dieting, such as muscle loss and low energy, apply.

angle.text: Losing body fat shows off your muscle and reduces aromatase activity, so less testosterone converts to estrogen. Reference text describes the aromatase mechanism and says weight loss may raise testosterone, though no clear BMI link has been found.

lead: Losing body fat to raise testosterone is the idea that getting leaner increases circulating testosterone in men, and with it the markers of a more masculine physique: more muscle definition, a harder look and an easier path to further muscle gain. Proponents link it to the way fat tissue handles sex hormones, so the practice appeals to people who are cutting for visible leanness and want the hormonal side effect as well.

Wikipedia reports that fat cells make the enzyme aromatase, which converts testosterone into estradiol, and that aromatase activity rises with obesity [1][2]. Its testosterone article states that weight loss may raise testosterone while also noting that no clear link between body mass index and testosterone has been found [1].

A 2024 meta-analysis of 44 studies and 1,774 men found that total and free testosterone rose after weight loss achieved by low-calorie diet or bariatric surgery, with larger gains in men who started with a higher BMI or lower testosterone [3]. A randomized trial in older men with obesity and low testosterone examined lifestyle therapy with and without testosterone replacement [3].

paras: The proposed pathway runs through aromatase, an enzyme present in fat tissue that converts testosterone into estradiol [1]. Wikipedia reports that aromatase activity increases with age, obesity, insulin and alcohol, so more fat tissue is associated with more conversion, and losing fat is proposed to reduce it [2]. Researchers also describe obesity-associated hypogonadism, in which low testosterone accompanies obesity and may improve with weight loss [3].

The testosterone article says weight loss may raise testosterone, while also reporting that no clear relationship between BMI and testosterone has been found [1]. The studies below look at men with obesity; findings in lean or normal-weight men are less documented.

A 2024 meta-analysis in Andrology pooled 44 studies with 1,774 participants: 19 used low-calorie diets and 26 used bariatric surgery. Total testosterone rose by about 2.5 nmol/L after diet-induced weight loss and 7.2 nmol/L after bariatric surgery, with a combined gain of 4.8 nmol/L, and free testosterone also rose. Gains were larger with higher baseline BMI or lower baseline SHBG and testosterone. Younger men (40 or under) gained less total but more free testosterone for a given weight loss, and the authors built nomograms to estimate the change [3].

A randomized, double-blind trial of 83 men aged 65 or older with obesity and low testosterone compared six months of lifestyle therapy (weight management and exercise) plus testosterone or placebo. With about 9 percent weight loss in both groups, lean mass and thigh muscle volume fell slightly less with testosterone, while physical performance improved similarly in both [3].

Wikipedia and the studies above do not report harms specific to fat loss for testosterone. The older-men trial noted that weight loss reduced lean mass and bone density to some degree, which testosterone partly attenuated [3].
